passages.title: About Craig
passages.text: Craig Michael Thompson 20+ years' experience in software development and management, from start-up to acquisition. I'm a hands-on, full-stack engineer across UI, back end, infrastructure and AI, with extensive engineering leadership experience. I led an engineering department to AI-first development, where most code is now generated by AI, then reviewed by AI and people. Problem solving is what I do best, whether the problem sits in the code, the platform or the team. I've led engineering teams for 12+ years, growing and developing teams of 10+ engineers, both in-house and outsourced. I've set strategy, supported the people and steered the platform with them, from monorepos and build engines to AWS, authentication and AI tooling. I've reported directly to CEO and CTO level, turning the roadmap and technical direction into plain-English board updates. I've been part of ISO 27001 and GDPR accreditation and the annual audits.

passages.title: ai.md: From AI-assisted to AI-first, in a year
passages.text: Over the past year I've led a radical change in how an engineering department works, from first introducing AI-assisted development to a point where the vast majority of code is generated by AI and reviewed by AI alongside human reviewers. It's checked against style and coding guidelines iterated on in the repo, so what's produced meets the team's standards rather than the model's defaults. Most code is now written by AI and checked by both AI and people before it merges. Standards live in the repo, so the models and the team work to the same rules. Reviewers know where to look before they open a diff. Chores like cost audits, dataset restores and stacked PRs are one command for any engineer or agent. passages.title: monorepo.md: One codebase, kept modern without stopping delivery
passages.text: // monorepo & developer experience · 2019; today One codebase, kept modern without stopping delivery I've taken a platform spread across about 18 separate repositories and led merging them into one TypeScript monorepo with their history intact, along with the tooling around it: CI/CD, Docker and local dev. That one codebase is what makes the repo-wide migrations in refactor.md possible. 2019 · 18 repositories ■ 12 services ■ React app ■ 3 Lambdas ■ Terraform ■ QA suite merged with full history; today · one monorepo 100+ packages today, including the shared React design system Every engineer works in one repo, with one toolchain and one way to build, test and deploy. Generated OpenAPI 3.1 docs for 12 services replaced a hand-maintained Postman collection.

passages.title: refactor.md: Keep the toolchain modern, one reviewed change at a time
passages.text: // refactors & tooling migrations Keep the toolchain modern, one reviewed change at a time Tooling ages fast. Rather than letting it drift, I've led a steady run of repo-wide migrations: linting, packages, bundling, types, runtime and the compiler itself. Each one was scripted with a codemod and landed as a single reviewed change, so there was never a long-lived branch or a half-migrated codebase. Repo-wide migrations I've led 9,700+ files moved across them linting TSLint; ESLint 455 files ci Semaphore; self-hosted Buildkite CI as code packages yarn; pnpm workspaces 619 files bundling Webpack; Vite 3 front ends types type aliases; interfaces 804-file codemod lint + format ESLint + Prettier; oxlint + oxfmt 4,366 files runtime compiled JS; TypeScript run natively by Node 3,502 files compiler TypeScript 5.8; TypeScript 7 ~10× faster typechecks e2e testing Cypress; Playwright faster, more stable CI Upgrades land across the repo in one change, so the codebase doesn't drift into "old" and "new". Back-end services start straight from TypeScript source, with no build step in between. Faster tools where it counts: one quick linter and formatter, and typechecks around 10× faster on TypeScript 7.

passages.title: ci-cd.md: Build only what changed, ship every merge
passages.text: // ci/cd & release engineering · 2019; today Build only what changed, ship every merge I built a CI/CD platform from scratch and have kept evolving it as the team and codebase grew. Today it runs on self-hosted Buildkite defined in Terraform, driven by an in-house TypeScript build-and-deploy engine. It models the monorepo's dependency graph, so each change builds and deploys only the packages it affects. Every merge to master, end to end ⎇ merge to master ▶ package graph what's affected? ▶ build in parallel affected packages only lib service app ▶ Validate gate format lint types tests drift ▶ staging auto-deploy ▶ production live, no release train How it evolved: pipelines; a graph-aware release engine started as: hosted pipelines then: Buildkite + build engine then: continuous deployment then: merge queue · staging today: one Validate gate Merged work reaches customers automatically. There has been no release train since 2022. A small fix rebuilds a handful of packages, not the whole platform. Every PR passes one required quality gate, and /deploy on a PR puts it into a test environment. Deploys wait for healthy tasks and detect rollbacks, so a bad release stops itself.

As it grew, its performance in CI suffered. after · Playwright Huge gains in performance and stability across CI/CD. Inception Led the creation of the first end-to-end automation suite, on Cypress. Evolving in CI Grew the suite inside the CI pipeline over time, alongside the Test Automation Engineers. The switch When performance suffered as the suite grew, led the move to Playwright. Automated end-to-end testing has been part of CI since the first suite. The suite was built up together with the Test Automation Engineers. Moving to Playwright made the suite much faster and more stable in CI/CD.

passages.title: aws.md: Nothing public but the CDN
passages.text: // aws architecture · 2021; 2026 Nothing public but the CDN I led the platform's move from containers on EC2 hosts behind a public load balancer to Fargate tasks that talk over ECS Service Connect, with all customer traffic entering through CloudFront and WAF. Each step shipped without a big-bang cutover. before · ~2020 Internet ↓ Public load balancer · internet-facing ↓ ECS on EC2 hosts · hosts to patch ↓ Database via VPC peering Operator access: SSH bastion after · 2026 Internet ↓ CloudFront + WAF · the only public entry ↓ Internal load balancer · private ↓ Fargate · Service Connect · no hosts ↓ Database via PrivateLink Operator access: SSO + SSM, no SSH How it evolved: hosts to patch; no hosts at all started as: ECS on EC2 hosts then: capacity autoscaling then: awsvpc networking then: Fargate rollout today: Fargate + Service Connect No servers to patch: every service runs on Fargate. The attack surface is one CDN. WAF moved to blocking only after a 14-day shadow run showed no legitimate traffic would be stopped. Each service receives only the events it handles, using subscription filters generated from its code at build time. Dev environments share one networking stack and one database cluster, so a new environment is cheap to stand up.

passages.title: security.md: Closing doors, not adding locks
passages.text: // security & privacy · 2021; 2026 Closing doors, not adding locks When a product handles confidential data, security and privacy are part of the product. We focused on removing whole classes of risk rather than layering controls on top. area before after server access SSH & bastions SSM Session Manager; port 22 closed everywhere admin access IAM admin users SSO only, via IAM Identity Center and Control Tower networks VPC peering PrivateLink and VPC endpoints public surface internet-facing load balancer One CDN entry point, with WAF in block mode dev secrets plaintext.env files Injected at runtime from a password manager dependencies known CVEs lingering Vulnerable packages swapped out; pentest findings fixed and tracked incidents ad hoc Blameless post-mortems, with runbooks and tooling as the fix Far fewer standing keys and passwords for anyone to leak. No servers reachable from the internet except through the CDN. External penetration-test findings were fixed in code and tracked to closure.

passages.title: auth.md: Sign-in that enterprises trust and users don't notice
passages.text: // authentication & identity · 2024; 2026 Sign-in that enterprises trust and users don't notice I led the replacement of a legacy, multi-tenant sign-in system with a new auth framework, rolled out organisation by organisation behind a per-tenant switch. Before that, we hardened the old one: expiring tokens, central signing and key rotation. Every sign-in, end to end sign-in request from a tenant domain ▶ resolve organisation from the host name ▶ choose a method SAML SSO magic link password ▶ 2FA enforced per org ▶ rate-limit check per identity ▶ session + signed token EdDSA · published keys rate limiting by identity, not just IP Separate buckets per user, email, token and IP, per organisation, so one noisy office network can't lock out everyone behind it. user email token IP zero-downtime key rotation Verifiers accept old and new keys during an overlap window, so signing keys rotate without logging anyone out. key v1 key v2 overlap How it evolved: legacy service; enterprise-grade sign-in started as: legacy auth service then: shared auth library then: expiring, rotated tokens today: new auth framework Enterprise customers sign in through their own identity provider and can require 2FA for everyone. Sign-in links in emails still work after Slack or Outlook previews them. Tokens expire and keys rotate on a schedule, with no forced logouts. Services can verify tokens themselves against published keys, ready for service-to-service auth.

passages.title: data.md: Making the flagship report fast at scale
passages.text: // data & performance · 2021; 2026 Making the flagship report fast at scale Reporting is often the first place a SaaS platform slows down: large aggregations sliced by many dimensions at once. I led the redesign of a core reporting data model and its queries on MongoDB, and we proved the new version matched the old one in production before switching over. before: work done at read time, on every request every response; unwind all facets; group everything; confidentiality in the query after: work moved to write time, reads stay lean facets denormalised on write; purpose-built collection; high-cardinality-first index; analytics-node read; confidentiality in code, cacheable 10× higher complexity ceiling for core reports 1–3 s search stalls removed from people lists under load ~8,000 records no longer loaded to open one dashboard V1 ⇄ V2 diff mode proved parity in production How it evolved: read-time work; write-time design started as: streamed bulk operations then: reporting rework then: purpose-built collection today: Atlas Search Large customers can slice results by far more demographics before hitting limits. Bulk operations on very large tenants stream records instead of loading them all into memory. Every environment, and every laptop, can restore a realistic "gold" dataset in one step.

passages.title: cost.md: Measure first, then cut
passages.text: // cloud cost · 2022; 2026 Measure first, then cut Every saving started with data: flow logs, utilisation history or a line in the bill. Each change landed with the numbers that justified it in the pull request. 1 · measure; 2 · attribute; 3 · change; 4 · verify Documented monthly savings ≈ $1.3k / month from the first three alone Container Insights: enhanced; standard $620/mo Duplicate CloudTrail trails removed $450/mo BI network: 3 AZs and NATs; 1 $270/mo VPC flow logs off (per account) $250/mo Also cut, from measured utilisation Traced ~1.2 TB/day of CI NAT traffic; replaced managed NAT with endpoints, image caching and fck-nat Halved CPU and memory on services idling at 1–3% CPU Right-sized Redis after 15 months under 4% CPU Non-production environments scale down every night Spend tracks real usage, and every cut has the evidence behind it on record. The NAT investigation became a reusable audit any engineer can rerun.

passages.title: ai/platform.md: AI where it earns its keep
passages.text: // ai platform · mastra + bedrock · 2024; 2026 AI where it earns its keep I helped introduce AI into the product: an agent service built with Mastra, running models through Amazon Bedrock in its own isolated AWS account, with an eval suite that runs in CI. How AI reaches the product product features that call AI in the core platform; isolated AWS account AI agent service Mastra agents & workflows TypeScript, like the rest of the platform ⇄ models Amazon Bedrock inside the same cloud as everything else every change: PR to the AI service; eval suite in CI; ships only if it passes AI features are built as agents and workflows in TypeScript, so any engineer on the team can work on them. The AI service has its own account, with its own permissions and its own bill, separate from the core platform. Changes to the AI service are checked by its eval suite in CI before they reach customers.

passages.title: FAQ: What roles are you open to?
passages.text: Hands-on technical leadership roles, such as Head of Engineering, where I stay close to the code and to AI-first delivery while setting direction for the team. I'm most at home in start-ups and scale-ups.

passages.title: FAQ: Remote, hybrid or office?
passages.text: Primarily remote. I'd consider hybrid for a North East–based company with genuinely flexible attendance, but not a fixed "X days a week" commitment.

passages.title: FAQ: Where are you based?
passages.text: Newcastle upon Tyne, UK.

passages.title: FAQ: What's your notice period?
passages.text: Three months.

passages.title: FAQ: How big a team have you led?
passages.text: Up to 12 engineers as Head of Engineering, and before that a Scrum team of junior-to-mid engineers as a Technical Lead.

passages.title: FAQ: Have you hired and grown engineers?
passages.text: Yes. I've hired 10+ engineers, through an interview process I designed with the CTO and Deputy Head. Many of the people I've led have been promoted, including one from Software Engineer to my Deputy Head of Engineering. See hiring.md and people.md.

passages.title: FAQ: Have you worked with customers and the board?
passages.text: Yes. I've joined sales, customer and due-diligence calls as the technical expert, been the primary escalation point for major customer issues alongside my Deputy, and reported to the CEO and CTO with board material in plain terms. See customers.md and product.md.

passages.title: FAQ: How do you use AI in engineering?
passages.text: Over the past year I've led an engineering department from introducing AI-assisted development to a point where the vast majority of code is AI-generated, then reviewed by AI alongside human reviewers against style and coding guidelines iterated on in the repo. See ai.md.

passages.title: FAQ: Have you owned a budget?
passages.text: Yes. I've owned the substantial monthly AWS budget for a SaaS platform, and managed the platform's technical suppliers and the wider IT suppliers, negotiating renewals and contracts. See budget.md.

passages.title: FAQ: Have you led incidents and on-call?
passages.text: Yes. I set up the on-call rota and status page, led on incidents from single-client issues to full outages, and helped produce the business's disaster recovery process. See incidents.md.

passages.title: FAQ: Do you cover internal IT too?
passages.text: Yes. I've been the point person for IT: the hardware estate, Google Workspace, the MDM that provisions and secures the Mac estate, and an IT service desk I set up for everyone. See it.md.

passages.title: FAQ: Have you worked with outsourced or offshore teams?
passages.text: Yes. As Head of Engineering I worked directly with an outsourcing firm in India, onboarding 5+ Software Engineers and Automation Test Engineers to bolster the in-house team. Many of them stayed for 2+ years.

passages.title: FAQ: Have you been through an acquisition?
passages.text: Yes. I've led engineering from startup through to acquisition, and represented engineering right through due diligence. See acquisition.md.

passages.title: FAQ: Are you still hands-on?
passages.text: Yes. Alongside setting strategy and leading the team, I've kept writing code; several of the upstream pull requests on this page are recent.

passages.title: FAQ: What industries have you worked in?
passages.text: Mostly B2B SaaS for enterprise customers, including an email marketing platform sending billions of emails, plus consulting for clients worldwide.

passages.title: FAQ: Do you have compliance experience?
passages.text: Yes: GDPR and ISO 27001 accreditation, the annual audits, and arranging the yearly penetration test. See compliance.md.

passages.title: FAQ: Which clouds do you know?
passages.text: Primarily AWS, with more limited exposure to GCP and Azure.

passages.title: FAQ: Can I get a copy of your CV?
passages.text: Yes. There's a plain, one-page version at craga.dev/cv that you can print or save as a PDF, or email me and I'll send it.
